questions.stem: 'Mistakes were made in the handling of the complaint.' What is the main effect of this grammatical choice?
options: It names the agent clearly but softens the seriousness of the mistakes
It turns the verb 'handle' into a noun so the process sounds ongoing
It makes the complainant the grammatical subject and gives them authority
It removes the agent, so no person is held responsible for the mistakes
questions.explanation: The passive voice allows the 'by ...' phrase naming the doer to be deleted, so the sentence reports an action with nobody attached to it — a classic way institutions avoid accountability. The option about nominalisation is tempting because 'handling' is indeed a nominalisation, but that is not the main effect here; the agent-deleting passive 'were made' does the work of hiding who acted. Ask first: does the sentence tell me who did it?

questions.stem: Which pair correctly matches a term with its meaning?
options: Modality: joining two independent clauses with a semicolon instead of a conjunction
Modality: replacing a noun group with a pronoun to keep a paragraph cohesive
Nominalisation: turning a verb or adjective into a noun, as in 'decide' becoming 'decision'
Nominalisation: naming the person responsible for an action in the subject position
questions.explanation: Nominalisation converts processes or qualities into nouns, which compresses information and often removes the doer from view. The option defining nominalisation as naming the responsible person reverses its usual effect — nominalisation typically strips agents out rather than putting them in. Modality refers to the degree of certainty or obligation in words such as 'must', 'might' and 'should', not to punctuation or reference.

questions.stem: A school newsletter changes 'Students must not enter the staff car park' to 'Let's all keep the staff car park clear.' What is the main social effect of the change?
options: The inclusive 'let's' raises the obligation so the instruction becomes more binding
The change removes all modality, so the sentence no longer expresses any expectation
The change makes students the excluded group by addressing only staff members
The inclusive 'let's' positions writer and students as one group sharing responsibility
questions.explanation: 'Let's' is the inclusive first person plural: it folds the writer into the group being asked to act, reducing the distance between authority and audience. The option about raising obligation is tempting because both versions ask for the same behaviour, but 'must not' is high modality and 'let's' is a softened invitation, so obligation drops rather than rises. Track who the pronoun includes and how strong the modal word is.

questions.stem: Which revision of 'the disabled' best reflects person-first inclusive language?
options: the differently abled group
people with disability
the disability community sufferers
disability-afflicted persons
questions.explanation: Person-first language places the noun for the person before the descriptor, so the person is not reduced to a single characteristic. 'The differently abled group' is tempting because it sounds gentle, but it is a euphemism that still labels a group rather than naming people first, and it is widely rejected by disability advocates. Look for the pattern 'people with ...' as the reliable person-first structure.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses high modality to assert the writer's authority most strongly?
options: The council may wish to release the report before the month is over
The council must release the report before the end of the month
The council might consider releasing the report before the end of the month
The council could perhaps release the report at some stage this month
questions.explanation: 'Must' sits at the top of the modality scale, expressing obligation with no room for negotiation, which projects the writer as entitled to make demands. The version with 'may wish to' is the closest rival because it sounds formal and official, but 'may wish to' is low modality that leaves the decision entirely with the council. Rank the modal word itself — must and will are high, may, might and could are low.

questions.stem: A student wants to rewrite 'Late assessment submissions will be penalised' so that responsibility is visible and students are addressed as capable decision-makers. Which rewrite best achieves this?
options: Late submission of assessment tasks results in the deduction of available marks
If you submit an assessment after the due date, your teacher will deduct marks
A penalty is applied to any assessment submission received after the due date
The application of penalties to late assessment submissions is standard practice
questions.explanation: The successful rewrite uses second person direct address and two named agents in active clauses — 'you submit' and 'your teacher will deduct' — so both the student's choice and the teacher's action are visible. The version beginning 'A penalty is applied' is the closest rival because it uses a full sentence with a verb, but 'is applied' is an agentless passive that still hides who imposes the penalty. Test each rewrite by asking whether a human doer appears as the subject of the verb.

questions.stem: An opinion column opens: 'As Australians, we all know that a fair go means rewarding effort, not handing out endless support.' What is the most accurate analysis of how this sentence uses language to include and exclude?
options: The inclusive 'we' builds a shared national identity, so readers who disagree are positioned as outside the group
The passive construction conceals who actually holds the view, so no reader is held responsible for it
The first-person plural weakens the writer's authority, so readers are invited to reject the claim
The nominalisation 'support' turns a process into a thing, so the claim becomes measurable and verifiable
questions.explanation: An inclusive 'we' assumes agreement before it is argued for: it enrols the reader into a group that supposedly already shares the value, so disagreeing means stepping outside 'Australians' as the writer has defined them. The option about passive construction is the most tempting because hiding agency is a real disempowering technique, but this sentence is in the active voice with 'we' clearly named as the subject, so nothing is concealed. Check the verb first — if there is a named subject doing the action, the effect is coming from pronoun choice, not from the passive.

questions.stem: What is 'evaluative language'?
options: Words that report an event neutrally, without naming anyone
Words that join clauses so a text flows from point to point
Words that name abstract processes by turning verbs into nouns
Words that convey judgement, appreciation or emotion
questions.explanation: Evaluative language positions a reader by attaching a positive or negative value to something — through judgement of behaviour, appreciation of qualities, or expression of feeling. The option about turning verbs into nouns describes nominalisation, which can hide agency but is not in itself evaluation. Joining clauses describes cohesive conjunctions, and neutral reporting is the opposite of evaluation. The cue is whether the word carries a value: 'reckless' evaluates, 'drove' does not.

questions.stem: What does it mean to say a writer 'substantiates' a claim?
options: The writer supports the claim with evidence such as data, examples, expert opinion or citation
The writer restates the claim more forcefully using stronger adjectives and higher modality
The writer softens the claim with hedging words so that it cannot easily be disputed
The writer attributes the claim to an unnamed group so that responsibility is shared
questions.explanation: To substantiate is to back a claim with grounds — evidence a reader could check, such as statistics, examples or a named authority. Restating the claim with stronger adjectives only intensifies it; intensity is not evidence, and this is the most common confusion in student analysis. Ask 'could a reader verify this?' — if not, the claim has been asserted, not substantiated.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains explicit rather than implicit evaluation?
options: The council closed the pool three days before the school holidays began.
Swimmers arriving on Monday found the gates chained and a printed notice taped up.
Since the closure, the nearest public pool has been a forty-minute bus ride away.
The council's decision to close the pool was irresponsible and short-sighted.
questions.explanation: Explicit evaluation states the judgement outright in words that carry value, such as 'irresponsible' and 'short-sighted'. The other sentences select and arrange facts — timing, chained gates, distance — so a reader is likely to infer criticism, but no evaluative word appears; that is implicit evaluation. The cue is whether you can point to the judging word itself.

questions.stem: An article describes a group of protesters as 'a mob that swarmed the intersection'. What view is most clearly revealed by this word choice?
options: That the protesters were an unruly threat rather than citizens exercising a right
That the protesters were numerous but their cause was reasonable and well organised
That the writer is reporting neutrally, since 'mob' and 'swarmed' simply describe a crowd
That the writer is substantiating a claim about the protest with observable evidence
questions.explanation: 'Mob' judges the group as disorderly and 'swarmed' likens them to insects, so the pairing constructs the protest as a threat to be contained rather than a legitimate act. The claim that these are neutral descriptive words is the trap: 'crowd gathered at the intersection' would be neutral, and comparing the two shows how much value the original carries. Descriptive colour is also not evidence, so nothing here substantiates a claim.

questions.stem: A newspaper writes: 'Experts agree that the new curfew has been a success.' Why is this weaker substantiation than it first appears?
options: No expert is named and no evidence for the success is given, so the claim rests on unverifiable authority
The word 'success' is too low in modality, so readers assume the writer is uncertain about the curfew
Naming a source is unnecessary in journalism, so the sentence substantiates the claim adequately
The sentence is implicitly evaluative, and implicit evaluation can never be supported by evidence
questions.explanation: Substantiation requires grounds a reader can trace: which experts, agreeing on what measure of success. An unattributed appeal to 'experts' borrows the prestige of authority without supplying anything checkable. The suggestion that the sentence substantiates adequately misunderstands attribution — even in journalism, an unnamed collective source gives the reader nothing to test. Note too that 'success' is an explicit evaluation, and explicit claims can certainly be supported by evidence when it is provided.

questions.stem: Two reports on the same council meeting begin: 'The council finally approved the housing plan after months of delay' and 'The council approved the housing plan after a lengthy period of community consultation.' What best explains how each reveals a value position?
options: The first is implicitly evaluative through 'finally', while the second contains no evaluation at all
Both select and evaluate the same time period, one framing it as obstruction and the other as due process
Both report the same neutral facts, and any difference in effect comes only from sentence length
The first substantiates its claim with evidence of delay, while the second offers only an opinion
questions.explanation: The identical stretch of time is renamed: 'months of delay', intensified by 'finally', judges the council as slow, while 'a lengthy period of community consultation' recasts the same wait as responsible process. The claim that the second contains no evaluation is the closest trap — 'community consultation' is itself an approving construal of what happened. Neither version supplies figures or sources, so neither substantiates anything; the values sit in the naming.

questions.stem: An editorial argues: 'Every reasonable person can see that the proposal must be rejected.' Which analysis of this sentence is accurate?
options: The phrase 'every reasonable person' functions as evidence, so the writer has substantiated the rejection of the proposal
The high modality of 'must' guarantees the claim is supported, since strong wording signals a well-researched position
The sentence is implicitly evaluative only, because it contains no words that directly judge people or ideas
High modality plus an evaluative label positions dissenters as unreasonable, so agreement is assumed rather than argued
questions.explanation: 'Must be rejected' asserts obligation at the highest modality, while 'every reasonable person' makes agreement a condition of being reasonable — the reader is enlisted before any grounds are offered. The suggestion that this counts as substantiation is the main trap: naming your audience as reasonable is a rhetorical move, not evidence. Note also that 'reasonable' is an explicit evaluative word, so the claim of purely implicit evaluation fails.

questions.stem: A student rewrites 'The council decided to close the pool, and residents were furious.' Which rewrite uses nominalisation?
options: The council must surely have known that closing the pool would enrage residents.
The council's decision to close the pool caused fury among residents.
It was decided by the council that the pool would be closed, angering residents.
The council decided to close the pool, so residents became furious.
questions.explanation: 'Decided' becomes the noun group 'the council's decision' and 'furious' becomes the noun 'fury', so two processes are packaged as things and joined by a single verb — that is nominalisation. The version beginning 'It was decided by the council' is tempting because it also sounds formal, but its change is to passive voice: the verb 'decided' stays a verb. Cue: look for a noun that could be turned back into a verb or adjective ('decision' → decide, 'fury' → furious).

questions.stem: Which statement about text connectives is correct?
options: 'However' signals a contrast between what has just been said and what follows
'Furthermore' signals a contrast between what has just been said and what follows
'Therefore' signals that an extra example is being added to the previous point
'Meanwhile' signals that the writer is conceding a point to the opposing side
questions.explanation: Text connectives build cohesion by naming the relationship between chunks of text, and 'however' marks a contrasting or concessive relationship. The option about 'furthermore' is the closest trap: 'furthermore' adds to and reinforces the previous point rather than opposing it. Cue: sort connectives into families — adding (furthermore, in addition), contrasting (however, nevertheless), causing (therefore, consequently), timing (meanwhile, subsequently).

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the semicolon correctly?
options: The trial ran for six months; the results were published in March.
The trial ran for six months; and the results were published in March.
The trial produced three findings; lower costs, faster service and fewer complaints.
Although the trial ran for six months; the results were published in March.
questions.explanation: A semicolon joins two independent clauses that are closely related in meaning, and both halves here could stand alone as sentences. The version with 'three findings; lower costs...' is the most tempting error: a list introduced by an announcement like that needs a colon, not a semicolon. Cue: check that what sits on each side of a semicolon would work as a complete sentence on its own.

questions.stem: In formal writing, what is the main job of a colon?
options: To set off extra, non-essential information that could be lifted out of the sentence
To introduce a list, explanation or example that follows from the statement before it
To join two complete sentences that a full stop would otherwise separate too sharply
To mark a sudden break in tone or an interruption in the flow of a sentence
questions.explanation: A colon points forward: the words before it make a statement, and what follows delivers the list, explanation or example that statement promised. The option about joining two complete sentences is tempting because a colon can sit between clauses, but that description belongs to the semicolon, where neither half explains the other. Cue: if the second part answers 'namely what?', use a colon; if it is simply a closely related second idea, use a semicolon.

questions.stem: A feature article builds a long, clause-heavy sentence describing years of planning, then follows it with: 'Nothing changed.' What is the most accurate analysis of this structural choice?
options: The short sentence lowers the modality of the passage, hedging the claim so readers can weigh the evidence themselves
The short sentence is a grammatical error in formal writing, since feature articles require sentences of even length
The abrupt shift to a short simple sentence creates emphasis by contrast, driving home the futility the long sentence has built up
The short sentence functions as a text connective, signalling to the reader that a new stage of the argument is beginning
questions.explanation: Sentence length is a stylistic resource: after a sprawling complex sentence, a blunt simple sentence lands with force because the rhythm breaks, and the contrast enacts the collapse of all that effort. The connective option is the closest distractor, but connectives are words such as 'however' or 'consequently' that name relationships, not whole sentences used for impact. Cue: ask what the reader feels at that point in the rhythm, then name the grammatical feature producing it.

questions.stem: In a complex sentence, what is the function of a subordinate clause?
options: It forms a complete sentence on its own and can be punctuated with a full stop without any change
It must always be placed at the start of the sentence and be followed by a comma
It adds supporting information such as time, reason or condition, while the main clause carries the central idea
It expresses an idea of equal weight to the main clause, joined by a coordinating conjunction such as 'and' or 'but'
questions.explanation: A subordinate (dependent) clause is grammatically dependent on a main clause; it supplies extra detail — when, why, although, if — while the main clause holds the key idea, which is why writers use it to rank information. The option describing ideas of equal weight joined by 'and' or 'but' is the most tempting, but that describes a compound sentence, where two main clauses are coordinated. The cue is the conjunction: subordinating words like 'because', 'although', 'while' create dependence, so the clause cannot stand alone, and it may appear before or after the main clause.

questions.stem: A news report is written using the 'inverted pyramid' structure. What does this mean about the sequence of information?
options: The report opens with background context and saves the key event for the final paragraph
Each paragraph is arranged from the longest sentence down to the shortest sentence
The most newsworthy information comes first, with supporting detail and background following
Events are told strictly in the order they happened, from earliest to most recent
questions.explanation: The inverted pyramid loads the essential who, what, where and when into the opening, then adds progressively less critical detail, so a reader who stops early still has the story. The strongest distractor is the strict chronological ordering, which describes a recount, not a news report; news deliberately breaks chronology to front the most significant fact. Cue: 'inverted' signals that importance, not time, drives the order.

questions.stem: Read this paragraph: 'The council trialled a night bus service last winter. It ran between the station and the university until 2 am. The trial was extended in March. This decision surprised residents.' Which cohesive device is doing most of the work of holding these sentences together?
options: Subordinate clauses embedded inside each of the four sentences
Contrasting connectives signalling a change in the direction of the argument
Direct repetition of exactly the same noun group in every sentence
Reference words ('It', 'This decision') pointing back to earlier information
questions.explanation: 'It' refers back to the night bus service and 'This decision' summarises the extension mentioned before it, so backward-pointing reference is the main tie between sentences. The repetition option is tempting because the topic stays constant, but no noun group is actually repeated identically across all four sentences. Cue: look for words that cannot be understood without checking what came earlier — those are reference ties.

questions.stem: A report explains how a bushfire started, spread and was contained. Which structure suits it?
options: Compare and contrast, because the report weighs two different fires against each other
Problem and solution, because the report proposes a policy to adopt
Inverted pyramid, because the report must open with a witness quotation
Chronological, because the purpose is to track one set of events through time
questions.explanation: Text structures are chosen to match purpose, and a report tracing one event unfolding over 12 hours is best sequenced in time order so causes and consequences follow each other clearly. Problem and solution is tempting because bushfires are a problem, but that structure exists to argue for a course of action, and this report is explaining what happened rather than recommending anything. Ask what the text is trying to do: explain a sequence, compare options, or propose action.

questions.stem: A student is writing a comparison of solar and wind power, and wants readers to weigh the two directly on cost, reliability and land use. Which organisation of the body paragraphs best serves that purpose?
options: All paragraphs on solar first, then all on wind, so that no criterion needs to be named
One paragraph per source with no criteria, because comparison happens only in the conclusion
Paragraphs ordered from longest to shortest, because length signals which points matter most
One paragraph per criterion, dealing with both solar and wind inside each paragraph
questions.explanation: When the purpose is direct comparison, organising by criterion places the two subjects side by side at each point, so the reader can judge them against the same measure without holding information in memory across the whole essay. The block option, which puts all of solar before all of wind, is tempting because it is tidy, but its reasoning is wrong: criteria still have to be named and matched, otherwise the two halves do not line up. Match structure to purpose: point-by-point for direct weighing, block only when each subject needs an extended standalone description.

questions.stem: Which describes a problem–solution text structure?
options: It states a position, then lists arguments from weakest to strongest
It sets out an issue and its consequences, then proposes and weighs responses
It presents two subjects in turn, covering the same criteria for each
It orders events strictly from earliest to latest, using time markers at each stage
questions.explanation: A problem–solution structure has two linked stages: the issue is defined and its effects made clear, and then one or more responses are put forward and evaluated. The option describing two subjects covered against the same criteria is a compare–contrast structure, which organises information by category rather than by trouble and remedy. Ask what the second half of the text is doing: if it proposes action, the structure is problem–solution; if it mirrors the first half, it is comparison.

questions.stem: A short story opens with the narrator standing in a burnt-out kitchen at the end of the events. The second paragraph begins: 'Three months earlier, the house had smelled of paint and possibility.' What is the most accurate analysis of this structural choice?
options: The writer varies chronological order to create suspense about how the ending came about, using a time marker to keep the sequence clear
The writer abandons cause and effect, so readers are meant to see the events as unconnected fragments rather than a sequence
The writer signals that the narrator is unreliable, since only unreliable narrators can describe events out of the order they happened
The writer replaces narrative structure with a recount structure, because the events are now being reported after they finished
questions.explanation: Starting at the outcome and then jumping back is a deliberate variation of sequence: the reader knows where things end up and reads on to find out why, while the explicit time marker 'three months earlier' preserves cohesion so the shift is not confusing. The claim that cause and effect is abandoned is tempting because the order is disturbed, but reordering events actually foregrounds causation by making the reader search for it. The cue is the time connective: writers who reorder events almost always signpost the shift so the sequence stays trackable.

questions.stem: A student has drafted a report for a busy council committee with the structure: background, research method, findings, recommendations. They decide to move the recommendations to the front, followed by a short summary of findings, then the detailed background and method. Which analysis of this restructuring is most accurate?
options: The structure has been varied in a way that removes the need for connectives, because the most important material is now first
The structure has been varied so the report becomes a persuasive text, since recommendations placed first always function as a thesis
The structure has been varied to suit readers who need decisions first, so extra signposting is needed to keep the later detail cohesive
The structure has been varied so that the report now has no sequence, since sequence only exists when information runs in time order
questions.explanation: Text structures are selected for purpose and audience: a committee that must act wants the recommendations up front, with supporting detail available afterwards. Because readers now meet conclusions before evidence, the writer must signpost clearly, referring back to each recommendation so the later sections stay tied to them. The option claiming there is now no sequence is tempting if sequence is thought of only as chronology, but sequence also means order of importance, category or logic. Remember that reordering a text changes which cohesive links the writer must supply, rather than removing the need for them.

questions.stem: Which of these is a compound sentence?
options: The students gathered their books and filed out of the hall.
The bell rang, and the students filed out of the hall.
When the bell rang, the students filed out of the hall.
The students filed out of the hall after the bell.
questions.explanation: A compound sentence joins two or more independent clauses (each able to stand alone) with a coordinating conjunction such as and, but or so. In the correct answer, 'The bell rang' and 'the students filed out of the hall' are both complete clauses. The most tempting wrong choice is the one with 'gathered their books and filed out' — the 'and' there joins two verbs sharing a single subject, so it is still one clause and therefore a simple sentence. Check whether the words on each side of the conjunction could each stand alone as a sentence.

questions.stem: When a sentence begins with a subordinate clause, which punctuation convention applies?
options: A semicolon is placed after the subordinate clause, before the main clause.
No punctuation is used, because the two clauses form one idea.
A colon is placed after the subordinate clause to introduce the main clause.
A comma is placed after the subordinate clause, before the main clause.
questions.explanation: A fronted subordinate clause, such as 'Although the funding was approved', is marked off with a comma so the reader can see where the main clause begins. The semicolon option is tempting because semicolons do separate clauses, but they join two independent clauses, and a subordinate clause cannot stand alone. Cue: if the opening words start with although, because, when, if or since, expect a comma, not a semicolon.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses parallel structure most consistently?
options: The new timetable promises shorter waits, cheaper fares and cleaner trains.
The new timetable promises shorter waits, fares that cost less and to clean the trains.
The new timetable promises shorter waits, and it will make fares cheaper, so trains are cleaner.
The new timetable, which promises shorter waits, will reduce fares and trains will be cleaner.
questions.explanation: Parallelism means items in a list share the same grammatical form; here three adjective-plus-noun phrases are matched, which gives the sentence rhythm and makes the list easy to absorb. The option mixing 'shorter waits', 'fares that cost less' and 'to clean the trains' is the closest trap: it lists three ideas but each takes a different grammatical shape, so the pattern breaks. Test parallelism by checking whether each listed item could follow the introducing verb on its own in the same form.

questions.stem: A memoir includes these lines: 'Smoke on the ridge. No warning, no siren.' What is the most accurate analysis of these sentence structures?
options: They are simple sentences whose subject and finite verb appear after the noun.
They are minor sentences with no finite verb, creating clipped, urgent pacing.
They are complex sentences whose subordinating conjunctions have been left out.
They are compound sentences in which the coordinating conjunction is implied.
questions.explanation: Minor sentences (fragments used deliberately) lack a finite verb but are punctuated as sentences; here they strip out everything but the images, which speeds the reading and mimics panic. Calling them compound sentences with an implied conjunction is tempting because of the paired phrases, but a compound sentence requires two independent clauses, and neither group of words contains a verb doing tense work. Cue: find the finite verb first — no finite verb means no clause, so the unit is a minor sentence.

questions.stem: A student wants to combine 'The oval will be resurfaced next term.' and 'The oval floods every winter.' so the flooding becomes embedded background detail. Which rewrite does this using a relative clause?
options: The oval, which floods every winter, will be resurfaced next term.
The oval floods every winter, so it will be resurfaced next term.
Flooding every winter, the oval will be resurfaced next term.
Because the oval floods every winter, it will be resurfaced next term.
questions.explanation: A relative clause begins with a relative pronoun such as which, who or that and is embedded inside the main clause to add detail without giving it equal weight. The version beginning 'Because the oval floods every winter' is the strongest distractor: it is a subordinate clause, but an adverbial one giving a reason, and it fronts the flooding rather than tucking it inside. Look for the relative pronoun and the pair of commas around the embedded information.

questions.stem: A writer uses short simple sentences: 'The torch died. He waited. The water rose.' What effect does that create?
options: A quickened pace and urgency, as each idea lands separately with nothing softening it
A formal, considered tone, as simple sentences suit academic and technical writing
A clear cause-and-effect chain, as each event is shown to produce the next one
A shift to an unreliable narrator, as simple sentences show he cannot be trusted to explain
questions.explanation: Short simple sentences strip out subordinate clauses and connectives, so each idea arrives in a separate, abrupt unit; readers move quickly from full stop to full stop, which builds pace and pressure. The cause-and-effect option is the most tempting, but causal links are carried by connectives such as 'so', 'because' or 'therefore' — with those removed, any link is only implied by sequence, not signalled by the structure. The cue: subordination and connectives build relationships between ideas, while stacked simple sentences build speed.

questions.stem: A student is writing an opinion piece opposing a new stadium and wants the cost to be the idea readers weigh most heavily. Which sentence structure best achieves this?
options: The new stadium will cost ratepayers $400 million, and it will create hundreds of jobs.
The new stadium will cost ratepayers $400 million. It will create hundreds of jobs.
Although the new stadium will create hundreds of jobs, it will cost ratepayers $400 million.
Although the new stadium will cost ratepayers $400 million, it will create hundreds of jobs.
questions.explanation: In a complex sentence, the main clause carries the weight and the subordinate clause is positioned as concession or background, so putting the jobs in the 'Although' clause and the cost in the main clause makes the cost the dominant idea. The version beginning 'Although the new stadium will cost ratepayers $400 million' is the trap: it mentions cost first, but demotes it to the subordinate clause so the jobs claim wins. The cue: ask which idea sits in the main clause, not which idea appears first.

questions.stem: A campaign speech ends: 'Whatever the cost, whatever the delay, whatever the objections from those who profit from the current system, the levy must be passed.' Which analysis of this sentence structure is most accurate?
options: Three independent clauses are joined by commas, so the sentence gives the cost, the delay and the objections equal status with the demand
The main clause opens the sentence and the repeated elements trail after it, so the demand is softened into a list of qualifications
The repeated construction puts the verb into the passive throughout, so the speaker avoids naming who must pass the levy
Three parallel subordinate elements delay the main clause, so the demand arrives last and carries the weight of everything conceded before it
questions.explanation: The three 'whatever' elements are subordinate: none can stand alone, and each concedes an obstacle before the main clause 'the levy must be passed' finally arrives, so the delayed ending lands with accumulated force — a periodic effect. The option claiming three independent clauses joined by commas is the most tempting, but 'whatever the cost' has no subject–verb pairing that could stand as a sentence, so it is subordinate, not independent. The cue is to test each chunk on its own: if it cannot stand alone, it is building pressure towards the main clause rather than sharing status with it. The option about the main clause coming first simply misreads the order, and only 'must be passed' is passive, not the repeated elements.

questions.stem: In language analysis, the term 'syntax' refers to:
options: the way words, phrases and clauses are arranged into sentences
the writer's choice of individual words and their connotations
the system of punctuation marks used to separate ideas
the rhythm and sound patterns created when a text is read aloud
questions.explanation: Syntax is sentence architecture — the ordering and combining of words, phrases and clauses, which shapes emphasis, pace and formality. The option about word choice and connotations describes diction (lexical choice), a different level of language; a writer can keep the same words and change the syntax entirely by reordering them. A useful cue: if the analysis is about order and structure, it is syntax; if it is about which word was picked, it is diction.

questions.stem: Which of these is a sentence fragment rather than a complete sentence?
options: She sprinted through the rain, the letter still in her hand.
The rain fell, and she sprinted with the letter in her hand.
Because the rain fell, she sprinted with the letter in her hand.
Sprinting through the rain with the letter still in her hand.
questions.explanation: A fragment lacks a finite verb and subject working together as an independent clause; 'Sprinting...' is a participial phrase with no main clause attached. The version beginning 'Because the rain fell' is tempting because it opens with a subordinating conjunction, but it goes on to supply the main clause 'she sprinted', so it is complete. The cue is to ask whether the string contains a subject plus a finite verb that could stand alone.

questions.stem: 'It was the deputy principal who cancelled the excursion.' Compared with 'The deputy principal cancelled the excursion', what does this structure do?
options: It turns a statement into a hedged claim, reducing the writer's certainty
It converts the verb into a noun so the event sounds like an abstract process
It uses a cleft structure to single out the deputy principal as the point of focus
It shifts the sentence into passive voice so the action seems to have no agent
questions.explanation: A cleft sentence splits one clause into two ('It was X who...') so that the element in the 'It was...' slot is spotlighted, often to correct or contrast with an assumption. The passive voice option is tempting because the sentence is longer and more roundabout, but the agent is not hidden — it is actually pushed into the most prominent position. Look for the frame 'It was ... who/that ...' as the signal of a cleft.

questions.stem: Which of these is a complex sentence?
options: The rising river forced the council to close the old timber bridge.
The river rose overnight and flooded the low-lying access road.
Because the river had risen overnight, the council closed the bridge.
The river rose overnight, and the council closed the bridge.
questions.explanation: A complex sentence joins a main clause to at least one subordinate clause, and here 'Because the river had risen overnight' cannot stand alone. The version joined by 'and' after a comma is tempting, but two clauses that could each stand alone linked by a coordinating conjunction make a compound sentence, not a complex one. The cue is the conjunction: subordinators such as because, although, when and while signal complexity, while and, but and so signal coordination.

questions.stem: A student wants to concede that an excursion fee is small while keeping the objection as the main point of the sentence. Which rewrite subordinates the concession?
options: The fee is only $5, but it will still keep some students at home.
The fee is only $5. It will still keep some students at home.
It will keep some students at home, and the fee is only $5.
Although the fee is only $5, it will still keep some students at home.
questions.explanation: Putting the concession into a subordinate clause introduced by 'although' grammatically demotes it, so the main clause carries the argument the writer wants readers to hold onto. The version using 'but' is the closest rival, but coordination with 'but' gives the two ideas equal grammatical status rather than subordinating one. The cue is the conjunction type: subordinators like although and while rank ideas, whereas but and and balance them.

questions.stem: Which of these groups of words is a main (independent) clause?
options: Because the ferry was cancelled
After the cancelling of the ferry
The suddenly cancelled morning ferry
The ferry was cancelled
questions.explanation: A main clause has a subject and a finite verb and makes complete sense standing alone: 'the ferry' is the subject and 'was cancelled' the verb, so it can be a sentence on its own. The most tempting wrong choice is 'Because the ferry was cancelled' — it does contain a subject and verb, but the subordinating conjunction 'because' makes it dependent on another clause to complete the meaning. The cue: if a group of words has a subject and verb but still leaves you waiting for the rest, a subordinator is holding it down.

questions.stem: A school report reads: 'The students' lockers were relocated over the holidays.' What does the placement of the apostrophe tell the reader?
options: One particular student is being referred to, and the lockers belong to that student
The word 'students' has been shortened, with a letter left out
The lockers are being described rather than owned by anyone
More than one student is being referred to, and the lockers belong to them
questions.explanation: For a plural noun already ending in s, possession is shown by adding an apostrophe after the s, so 'students'' means 'belonging to the students' (plural). The tempting answer is the singular reading, but a single owner would be written 'the student's lockers', with the apostrophe before the s. The cue is where the apostrophe sits relative to the s: before it means one owner, after it means more than one.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'The new timetable — announced without warning on a Friday — has confused staff and students', what is the pair of dashes doing?
options: Introducing a list of items that follows a complete statement
Showing that words have been left out of a quoted passage
Setting off an interrupting comment inside the sentence with added emphasis
Joining two closely related independent clauses without using a conjunction
questions.explanation: A matched pair of dashes brackets off extra information in the middle of a sentence, and does so more emphatically than commas or parentheses, which push the aside into the background. Joining two independent clauses without a conjunction is the job of a semicolon, not a pair of dashes. The cue is that dashes come in a pair here and the sentence still reads as a complete unit if the material between them is removed.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a comma splice?
options: Because the bus was late, we walked to the station instead
The bus, which was late again, left us walking to the station
The bus was late, we walked to the station instead
The bus was late, so we walked to the station instead
questions.explanation: A comma splice occurs when a comma alone joins two independent clauses; 'The bus was late' and 'we walked to the station instead' can each stand alone, so they need a full stop, semicolon or coordinating conjunction. The version with 'so' is tempting because it looks similar, but the coordinating conjunction after the comma makes the join grammatical. Check whether the words on both sides of the comma could each be a sentence, and whether a joining word is present.

questions.stem: In an essay, a student writes: The principal said the trial was 'successful ... but expensive to sustain'. What does the ellipsis indicate?
options: The student is unsure of the principal's exact wording
The principal paused for a long time while speaking
The quotation continues for several more sentences afterwards
Words from the original quotation have been left out at that point
questions.explanation: Inside a quotation, an ellipsis marks material omitted from the source so the quote stays concise while remaining accurate. The 'paused while speaking' reading is tempting because ellipses do show hesitation or trailing off in narrative dialogue, but in cited evidence the convention is omission. The cue is the context: quoted evidence in an essay means words removed, dialogue in fiction means a pause or fade.

questions.stem: A feature writer drafts: 'The launch had been promoted for months. Nobody came.' The final version reads: 'The launch had been promoted for months: nobody came.' What does the colon do here?
options: It signals that the two statements are simply of equal importance
It marks the second statement as a direct quotation from an observer
It shows the second statement contradicts and cancels the first
It presents the second statement as the outcome that the first leads into
questions.explanation: A colon between clauses points forward, framing what follows as the explanation, result or payoff of what precedes it, so the emptiness reads as the consequence of all that promotion. The 'equal importance' option describes a semicolon, which balances two clauses rather than making one deliver on the other. Ask which way the punctuation points: a semicolon holds two ideas side by side, a colon aims the reader at the second.

questions.stem: A news feature reports: The council's 'consultation' with residents lasted twenty minutes. What is the writer signalling by putting single quotation marks around the word consultation?
options: Title — the word names an official document produced by the council
Distance and scepticism — the writer doubts that the process deserves that name
Accuracy — these are the exact words spoken aloud by a named council officer
Definition — the word is a technical term explained elsewhere in the report
questions.explanation: Quotation marks placed around a single ordinary word (often called scare quotes) hold the word at arm's length, inviting readers to question whether it is the right label. The most tempting wrong answer is that they mark the exact words of a speaker: direct quotation normally involves a full phrase or sentence with a reporting verb such as 'said', not one isolated noun. The cue is the single word with no attribution — that almost always signals irony rather than reported speech.

questions.stem: Compare these two sentences: (1) 'The players who were injured did not travel to Perth.' (2) 'The players, who were injured, did not travel to Perth.' Which statement about the effect of the commas is correct?
options: Sentence 1 says all the players were injured; sentence 2 says only the injured ones stayed home
Both sentences carry the same meaning, but sentence 2 simply reads more formally
Sentence 2 is incorrectly punctuated, because a 'who' clause never takes commas
Sentence 2 says all the players were injured; sentence 1 says only the injured ones stayed home
questions.explanation: Commas around a relative clause make it non-defining: the clause adds extra information about the whole group, so in sentence 2 the entire squad was injured. Without commas the clause is defining — it narrows 'the players' down to a subgroup, as in sentence 1. The tempting reversal is to think the commas single out a subgroup; remember that commas fence the clause off as an aside, and an aside cannot be doing the job of narrowing.

questions.stem: A journalist drafts: 'The report (which cost $2 million) recommended no change at all.' In the final version this becomes: 'The report — which cost $2 million — recommended no change at all.' What is the most accurate analysis of this change?
options: The information is identical, but dashes foreground the aside for emphasis where brackets play it down
The dashes make the cost detail grammatically essential, so the sentence now collapses without it
The brackets were an error, since a relative clause beginning with 'which' cannot sit inside brackets
The dashes turn the aside into a separate sentence, so it now needs a capital letter and full stop
questions.explanation: Brackets and paired dashes both enclose parenthetical material, but they carry different tone: brackets whisper the detail, while dashes interrupt the sentence and throw weight onto what they enclose — useful when the cost is the point. The tempting option is that the dashes make the clause essential; enclosed material is by definition removable, and the sentence still works without it whichever marks are used. The cue is that punctuation here changes emphasis and tone, not grammatical status.

questions.stem: What does the term 'inclusive language' most accurately refer to?
options: Word choices that avoid emotional appeals so the writing stays neutral and factual
Word choices that avoid assumptions about groups and allow readers to see themselves represented
Word choices that keep sentences short so that younger readers can follow the argument easily
Word choices that add technical vocabulary so specialists feel respected by the writer
questions.explanation: Inclusive language is about who is acknowledged and represented: it avoids terms that assume a default gender, background or ability, so a wider range of readers is positioned as belonging. The option about short sentences confuses inclusiveness with readability — a text can be simple to read and still exclude groups through its assumptions. The cue is that inclusion concerns social positioning of people, not sentence difficulty or tone.

questions.stem: A council notice reads: 'Errors were made in processing the applications.' How does this passive construction affect the reader's sense of responsibility?
options: It makes the errors sound deliberate, since passive voice always implies intention
It shifts responsibility onto the applicants, because they are the subject of the sentence
It removes the agent, so no person or body is named as responsible for the errors
It names the council as the agent, but places that information at the end for emphasis
questions.explanation: An agentless passive lets a writer state that something happened without saying who did it, which quietly protects the party at fault. The suggestion that the council is named at the end is wrong — there is no 'by the council' phrase anywhere in the sentence. The cue is to ask 'by whom?': if the sentence cannot answer, the agent has been deleted.

questions.stem: A hospital letter states: 'The termination of the visiting arrangement will occur on Monday.' What is the main social effect of using the nominalisation 'termination' rather than 'we will end'?
options: It makes the letter more inclusive, since abstract nouns address all readers equally
It identifies the hospital as responsible more clearly than a verb form would
It hides the decision-maker and makes the change seem like an event rather than a choice
It makes the decision sound temporary, because nouns describe states rather than actions
questions.explanation: Nominalisation turns a process into a thing, and in doing so it usually drops the person doing the action, so the change reads as something that simply occurs. The claim that it identifies the hospital more clearly is the reverse: 'we will end' names the actor, while 'the termination' does not. The cue is that abstract nouns like termination, closure or reduction often signal a missing human agent.

questions.stem: Which rewrite of 'Disabled people can access the ramp at the rear entrance' best reflects person-first inclusive language conventions?
options: People with disability can use the ramp at the rear entrance
The disabled are able to use the ramp at the rear entrance
Sufferers of disability may access the ramp at the rear entrance
Those unfortunate enough to need the ramp may use the rear entrance
questions.explanation: Person-first wording places the person before the condition, so identity is not reduced to a single characteristic. 'The disabled' is the most tempting distractor because it sounds neutral, but turning an adjective into a collective noun labels a whole group by one attribute. Words such as 'sufferers' and 'unfortunate' add pity, which positions people as passive rather than capable.

questions.stem: A tenancy notice reads: 'Occupants failing to comply may be subject to remedial action pursuant to clause 14.' Which analysis of the disempowering effect of this wording is most accurate?
options: Dense nominalisation and legal phrasing obscure what will actually happen and to whom
The short sentence length gives readers too little detail to understand their rights
The use of second person makes readers feel personally attacked by the landlord
The imperative mood commands readers without explaining the reason for the rule
questions.explanation: Phrases like 'remedial action' and 'pursuant to clause 14' package concrete consequences into abstract nouns and legalese, so a reader cannot easily tell who will do what. The claim about second person is false: the notice uses the third-person 'occupants', which is part of the distancing effect. The cue is to try rewriting the sentence with a person as subject and a plain verb — if that is hard, the original is hiding something.

questions.stem: Two headlines cover the same event: 'Police clashed with demonstrators' and 'Demonstrators clashed with police'. What best explains the difference in effect?
options: The second headline is more objective, because groups of citizens are named first
Subject position foregrounds one party as the initiator, shaping who seems responsible
Only the second is grammatically active, so it assigns responsibility more strongly
The verb 'clashed' changes meaning with word order, so the two describe different events
questions.explanation: Both sentences are active and use the same verb, so the only variable is which party occupies the subject slot — and readers tend to read the subject as the one who acted first. The claim that only the second is active is false: both have a subject, verb and object in the same pattern. The cue is to swap the noun phrases and notice that the grammar is unchanged while the implied blame shifts.

questions.stem: An opinion piece describes a proposed skate park as 'a much-needed space for young people' and describes those opposing it as 'a handful of residents worried about noise'. Which analysis of the evaluative language is most accurate?
options: Both phrases report verifiable detail about the proposal and the objectors, so the writer's own position on the skate park remains undisclosed
Both phrases substantiate the writer's claim with evidence rather than evaluate it, so the writer's values appear only in the concluding paragraph
'Much-needed' explicitly judges the park as beneficial, while 'a handful' implicitly minimises the opposition, together positioning readers to back the project
'Much-needed' implicitly judges the park as beneficial, while 'a handful' explicitly states the number of objectors, so no view of the opposition is offered
questions.explanation: Evaluative language can judge something openly or smuggle a judgement in through word choice: 'much-needed' is an outright positive appraisal, while 'a handful' does not count anyone but quietly frames the objectors as few and therefore easy to dismiss. The option calling 'a handful' an explicit statement of number is the tempting one, but it gives no figure at all — it is a loaded estimate whose work is to shrink the opposition's importance. The cue: if a word could be swapped for a neutral equivalent ('some residents', 'proposed space') and the feeling of the sentence changes, the original is carrying evaluation.

questions.stem: What is a clause?
options: A single word acting as a sentence
A phrase introduced by a preposition
A group of words with a subject and a verb
A group of words that contains no verb at all
questions.explanation: A clause is built around a subject and its verb, which is what lets it carry a complete idea. A phrase has no verb, and that missing verb is the quickest way to tell the two apart.
questions.teaching:
Sentences are built from units, and the units have names that get used loosely in conversation but precisely in grammar.

A phrase is a group of words working together without its own verb — "under the old bridge", "the tall woman in the coat". Add a verb and something doing it, and the unit becomes capable of expressing a complete idea: "the bridge collapsed". That combination is what this question is about, and it is the building block sentences are classified by. Some can stand alone as sentences; others begin with a word like "although" or "because" and cannot. The presence of a verb with its own subject is the test.

questions.stem: What does a semicolon do?
options: Separates a title from its subtitle
Joins two closely related independent clauses
Introduces a list that follows a complete clause
Marks where a word has been left out
questions.explanation: A semicolon links two clauses that could each stand alone but belong together. Introducing a list is the colon's job, and that is the usual confusion between the two marks.
questions.teaching:
The semicolon sits between a full stop and a comma in strength. A full stop separates two ideas completely; a comma is usually too weak to hold two complete statements together on its own.

Its main use links statements that could each have stood as a sentence, where they are so tightly connected that a full stop would break the thought. "The tide turned; the boat swung round." Write those as two sentences and you lose a little of the link. It has a second, rarer job separating items in a list when the items themselves already contain commas. What it does not do is introduce anything — announcing a list or an explanation belongs to the colon, and swapping the two is the usual error.

questions.stem: What is the passive voice?
options: The subject receives the action rather than doing it
The subject performs the action of the verb
The verb describes an ongoing state rather than an action
The sentence gives a command to the reader
questions.explanation: In the passive, the thing acted on becomes the subject: 'the window was broken'. The active voice is the tempting opposite, where the subject does the acting. Passive is useful when the doer is unknown or unimportant.
questions.teaching:
Compare two sentences carrying identical information. "The council closed the pool." "The pool was closed by the council." The first puts the doer at the front. The second moves the pool to the front, even though the pool did nothing — something was done to it.

That reversal is the whole grammatical difference, and it is worth spotting because writers reach for it deliberately. It lets you leave the doer out completely: "the pool was closed" names nobody at all. Sometimes that is honest and useful — in a science report, "the mixture was heated" keeps attention on the method rather than the student. Sometimes it conceals responsibility, which is why "mistakes were made" is such a notorious phrase. When you meet it in a text, ask who has vanished and whether that was the point.

questions.stem: What is a conjunction?
options: A word that describes a noun
A word that replaces a noun
A word that shows position in space
A word that joins clauses or phrases
questions.explanation: Conjunctions join: 'and', 'but', 'because', 'although'. A word that replaces a noun is a pronoun and a word showing position is a preposition, so each wrong option names a real part of speech doing a different job.
questions.teaching:
Every option here names a real part of speech, so the task is matching each name to its job rather than spotting one obvious fake.

A word describing a noun is an adjective. A word standing in for a noun is a pronoun. A word showing position or relationship — under, before, with — is a preposition. And a word whose whole purpose is to link things together is what this question asks about: "and", "but", "or" join equal parts, while "because", "although" and "while" attach a dependent part to a main one. That second group is exactly what turns two simple sentences into a complex one.

questions.stem: What does the apostrophe show in 'the dog's bowl'?
options: Possession
A plural
A contraction
An abbreviation
questions.explanation: Here the apostrophe shows the bowl belongs to the dog. Apostrophes do also mark contractions, as in 'don't', which is why that option tempts — but they never make a word plural.
questions.teaching:
The apostrophe has two jobs in English, and confusing them causes more written errors than any other punctuation mark.

One job marks missing letters: "do not" becomes "don't", with the mark standing where the o was. The other shows that something belongs to someone — and that is what is happening when the bowl belongs to the dog. Neither job is making a word plural, which is the error behind "banana's for sale". The classic trap is "its" and "it's": the first is possessive with no mark, the second is a contraction of "it is", which reverses the usual pattern.

questions.stem: What is a modal verb?
options: A verb formed from an adjective
A verb showing possibility or obligation
A verb describing a physical action
A verb that links a subject to a describing noun
questions.explanation: Modals such as 'must', 'might' and 'should' express how certain or how obliged something is. They are what lets a writer soften a claim to 'this may suggest' rather than 'this proves'.
questions.teaching:
Some verbs describe actions — run, build, eat. A small group does something different: rather than naming an action, they alter how certain or how necessary the action is.

"You must go", "you might go", "you could go" and "you should go" all describe the same action with completely different weight behind it. That is the whole function of this group, and it is why they matter in analysis: they are how a writer signals confidence. A scientist writing "this may suggest" is claiming much less than one writing "this proves", and an advertisement writing "you need this" is doing something quite deliberate.

questions.stem: What is a noun group?
options: A group of nouns that share a single plural form
A noun plus the words that describe it
Two nouns joined by a conjunction
A noun used as the object of a verb
questions.explanation: A noun group is the head noun with its modifiers — 'the badly cracked window'. Packing detail into noun groups is how writers add precision without adding sentences.
questions.teaching:
A noun on its own carries very little: "dog". Writers rarely leave it there, and the machinery for adding detail is what this term names.

Around the head noun you can stack articles, adjectives, and phrases that follow it: "the enormous grey dog from next door". All of that is one unit doing the job of a single noun in the sentence. It matters for analysis because packing detail here is how writers add precision without adding sentences — and it is where loaded language hides. "The protesters" and "the violent mob of protesters" occupy the same slot and do very different work.

questions.stem: What is a complex sentence?
options: Two main clauses joined by 'and' or 'but'
A single clause with several long phrases
A sentence that contains more than twenty words in total
One main clause plus at least one subordinate clause
questions.explanation: A complex sentence has a main clause and at least one subordinate clause depending on it. Two main clauses joined by 'and' make a compound sentence, which is the near-miss. Length has nothing to do with it.
questions.teaching:
A clause is a chunk of language with its own subject and verb. Sentences get classified by how many clauses they contain and how those clauses relate to each other.

Some clauses stand alone perfectly well: "the river rose". Others cannot — "although the river rose" leaves you waiting, because that opening word makes it depend on something else to finish the thought. Join two of the standing-alone kind with "and" or "but" and you get one classification. Attach a dependent chunk to a standing-alone one and you get a different classification, which is the one being asked about here. Length is irrelevant: a forty-word sentence can be a single clause, and a six-word one can hold two. Find the joining word and ask whether each piece could survive by itself.
